name: 4th Sunday of Lent
description: Sunday of Joy (Laetare). The Bread from Heaven.
biblicalBasis: The miracle of the loaves where Jesus feeds five thousand with five loaves and two fish (John 6:1-15, Matt 14:13-21). The Bread of Life discourse: "I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never go hungry" (John 6:35). Exodus 16 regarding the manna God gave the people in the wilderness. Psalm 78:24-25 concerning the bread from heaven.
significance: In the middle of Lent's desert journey, God provides abundance—just like the manna in the wilderness. Jesus breaks five loaves and feeds thousands, with twelve baskets left over. He is himself the manna—the bread of life that satisfies the soul's hunger. The miracle points to the Eucharist: the broken bread that gives fellowship with God.
liturgicalContext: Called "Laetare" after Isaiah 66:10: "Rejoice with Jerusalem!" Some traditions use rose color on this Sunday—a break of joy in the midst of Lenten purple, parallel to Gaudete in Advent. Lent has now reached its midpoint.
history: Laetare Sunday has been celebrated since the 4th century. In the Middle Ages it was called "Rose Sunday" because the pope blessed a golden rose. The custom of using rose-colored liturgical textiles dates back to the 12th century.
otConnections: The manna in the wilderness (Exod 16)—the bread from heaven that God gave daily. Elijah who was fed by angels in the wilderness (1 Kings 19:4-8). Elisha's miracle of the loaves where twenty barley loaves fed a hundred men with food left over (2 Kings 4:42-44)—a direct foreshadowing of Jesus' miracle.

references.reason: The day is about God's abundance and the bread from heaven. The text that the Father gives good gifts to those who ask emphasizes God's generous nature and trust that He will give what we need, even in the midst of Lent's desert journey.
The miracle of the loaves is the main text for the 4th Sunday of Lent (Laetare). The text concerns Jesus as the "bread of life" who feeds in the wilderness and is central to today's liturgy.
